episodes.205216: Within cool northeasterly surface flow, several upper-level disturbances tracked across central North Carolina from a persistent weak trough of low pressure over the Ohio Valley region. Copious amounts of moisture remained from the 5th of August. A wedge front was also in place along Interstate 95. Several reports of flash flooding were reported over the eastern Piedmont and northern Coastal Plain, including two fatalities in Nash County.
episodes.205358: Scattered thunderstorms produced locally heavy rainfall.
episodes.205454: Excessive rainfall develop from slow moving storms that tended to train over the same area. Precipitable water values were an excessive 2.2 inches.
episodes.205479: A cluster of thunderstorms produced heavy rain and localized flash flooding over parts of southeast North Dakota during the evening. A wake low developed as this complex moved east with widespread 50 to 55 mph winds reported, and one brief high wind report of 58 mph at Fargo Airport.
episodes.205570: Another round of locally heavy rain across the Upper Big Sioux Basin resulted in downstream minor flooding along portions of the Middle Big Sioux River.
episodes.205602: A front was just north of the local area with southwest steering flow in place. The front edge closer through the day, with an influx of moisture from the Gulf and steepening lapse rates aloft with the approach of a mid level trough. Diurnal heating combined with high moisture produced sea breezes, with a merger across inland northeast Florida in the late afternoon where a few strong to pulse severe storms developed. Weaker storm motion enabled slow moving storms which produced localized flooding rainfall.
episodes.206577: A line of storms produced large hail and high winds during the afternoon and evening of August 5th, and into the early morning hours of August 6th. The largest sized hail measured at 3 inches in diameter was observed in Hoven. Later in the evening, a peak wind gust of 99 mph was recorded on a weather station out at Sandy Shore State Park, while the Watertown Regional Airport ASOS would record a peak gust of 68 mph. Over 40 trees were topped or downed as a result of these winds around the Lake Kampeska area. Additional sporadic tree and crop damage was noted elsewhere across northeast South Dakota. ||Heavy rainfall would also lead to flooding with reports of several roads overtopped by water in the city of Watertown, the towns of Britton, Agency Village, and Wilmot, as well as portions of rural Codington, Roberts, and Marshall counties. Already saturated soils from a wet spring and summer were unable to absorb the 2 to 4 inches of rainfall, with the COOP observer in Wilmot measuring 3.63 inches and 3.31 inches of rainfall from a CoCoRaHS observer 1 mile south southeast of Kidder. These heavy rains would result in river flooding, mainly across the Big Sioux and its tributaries.
episodes.206605: Surface ridging over the peninsula south of a stationary boundary stalled over the panhandle lead to light flow and a weak sea breeze setup that produces gusty marine winds over the southern Tampa Bay waters.
episodes.206666: A shortwave trough and closed low reached the Quad State from the northwest during the morning of the 4th. The arrival of the shortwave preceded peak heating by several hours, limiting convective potential. Shear was very weak and instability limited. Slow-moving storms produced heavy rain, and multiple trees blown down in Delta by straight-line winds.
episodes.206710: A weak upper-level low pressure disturbance over Vancouver Island and an antecedent frontal boundary facilitated a period of showery post-frontal convection on the afternoon of August 6th. This activity was robust enough produce an isolated and short lived Landspout.
episodes.206745: Heavy rainfall of 2 to 4 inches across Codington and Hamlin counties, falling on already saturated soils due to above normal precipitation through the spring and summer months, resulted in flooding of the Big Sioux River and its tributaries including Mud and Willow Creeks. Flooding would mainly be limited to low spots and agricultural lands, however.
episodes.206764: Waterspout activity developed with evening showers and thunderstorms that moved offshore into the Gulf waters on the late afternoon and early evening of August 6, 2025.
episodes.206786: Thunderstorms moving offshore produced strong wind gusts along and offshore from the coast.
episodes.206818: A strong upper level wave moved from the northern Rockies into southern Canada, brushing through eastern South Dakota and stirring up a 35-45 knot low-level jet within an environment with around 2000 J/kg of elevated MUCAPE. By evening, a well-organized convective system developed across northeast South Dakota and dropped slowly southeast through the overnight hours. Along the track, stronger cells produced large hail up to golf ball size and scattered wind damage.
episodes.206819: A strong upper level wave moved from the northern Rockies into southern Canada, brushing through eastern South Dakota and stirring up a 35-45 knot low-level jet within an environment with around 2000 J/kg of elevated MUCAPE. By evening, a well-organized convective system developed across northeast South Dakota and dropped slowly southeast into southwest Minnesota and northwest Iowa through the overnight hours. Along the track, stronger cells produced large hail up to golf ball size and scattered wind damage.
episodes.206822: A strong upper level wave moved from the northern Rockies into southern Canada, brushing through eastern South Dakota and stirring up a 35-45 knot low-level jet within an environment with around 2000 J/kg of elevated MUCAPE. By evening, a well-organized convective system developed across northeast South Dakota and dropped slowly southeast into southwest Minnesota and northwest Iowa through the overnight hours. Along the track, stronger cells produced large hail up to golf ball size and scattered wind damage.
episodes.206823: A few thunderstorms developed along an outflow from overnight storms, with a very isolated stronger updraft briefly able to produce up to quarter size hail.
episodes.206896: A surface front and mid-level energy encountering a moderately unstable and deep moisture environment led to thunderstorms capable of producing damaging winds and heavy rainfall across Southeast South Carolina.
episodes.207058: Storms developed along the Black Hills just to the west and south of Sturgis during the rally. A storm coming off the Black Hills was able to produce a funnel cloud on the west side of Rapid City that had a lot of exposure.
episodes.207091: An upper-level trough and jet streak approached the Carolinas and Mid-Atlantic region on August 6. Despite the cool airmass in place, overrunning precipitation produced occasional moderate to heavy rainfall rates and flash flooding across portions of interior southern Virginia.
episodes.207227: Persistent low-level moisture and weak convergence along a stalled frontal boundary once again supported the development of scattered showers and thunderstorms over the coastal waters. Within this environment, a couple of waterspouts were reported. One occurred over Lake Pontchartrain and another observed south of Grand Isle. Both waterspouts remained over water and dissipated within several minutes. No damage or injuries were reported.
episodes.207228: Persistent low-level moisture and weak convergence along a frontal boundary that had been stalled over the local area for days once again supported the development of scattered showers and thunderstorms. Model soundings indicated a dry slot aloft along the northern periphery of much more moisture to the south. It was here that a storm was able to capitalize on that setup and produce a severe downburst of winds.
episodes.207543: Iowa was on the edge of a deep thermal ridge. Several weak embedded waves moved across, aiding in thunderstorms development as the interacted with the low level jet through the early morning. These early morning storms did remain sub severe, but produced heavy rain that continued through midday. Training storms across southern Iowa result in an area of five to seven plus inches of rain, but no flash flooding occurred there. Three plus inches of rain occurred in parts of Clarke, Decatur, and Wayne counties with culverts and secondary roads washed out in flash flooding. A single storm in southern Iowa strengthened as it was preparing to cross the border into Missouri. While it did not produce widespread severe damage, it did produce a microburst over the small town of Lineville, IA. A review of damage photos and drone footage provided by the Emergency Manager are consistent with straight line or microburst winds estimated of up to 90 mph. The damage footprint impacted outbuildings on the north end of Lineville and grain bins in south Lineville (a roughly 1 mile swath); as well as damage to trees and destruction of the fire station damage in between. The damage pattern in-town and in cornfields upstream did not reveal a focused track; instead a more erratic and fanning out pattern typical of severe straight line winds.

events.narrative: The WeatherFlow station at Parrish Park North measured a peak wind gust of 36 knots from the northwest at 19:25 LST. Earlier, a gust to 35 knots occurred at 19:20 LST.
A couple trees were downed by thunderstorm winds in Delta.
The Leola fire department observed a brief touchdown in an open field. No damage was observed.
A caller stated that multiple large tree branches had come down at Lee Park golf course.
Photos sent by the public included several large tree limbs down and plants in the garden flattened.
The Marshall county Emergency Manager reported street flooding in and around Britton. The CoCoRaHS observer 1 mile south southwest of Kidder recorded 3.31 inches of moisture.
Hail up to three inches in diameter was observed in Hoven. Several other reports of hail between 1.00 and 2.75 inches were received.
Thunderstorm wind gusts estimated at 60 mph resulted in broken branches.
Flash flooding reported in Fargo, ND.
A trained spotter reported that hay bales had rolled across highway 12 due to thunderstorm winds.
Street flooding in Fargo. 25th Street had two feet of water on it.
Widespread street flooding reported in Fargo. Vehicle stalls reported across the  metro area.
Images posted to social media of multiple uprooted trees near Lake Kampeska, including one that landed on a garage. A nearby weather station recorded a 99 mph wind gust.
A peak wind gust of 99 mph was recorded by a personal a weather station at Sandy Shore State Park.
The Watertown Regional Airport Automated Surface Observing System (ASOS) recorded a peak gust of 68 mph.

The Codington County Emergency Manager called in to report at least 40 large pines had been uprooted or knocked over along the south side of Lake Kampeska. One of these trees fell on a substation and power was knocked out to portions of Watertown for a few hours.
A several minute period of severe thunderstorm winds with a peak gust of 61 mph was measured by a Road Weather Information System site 13 miles west of Ward.
A trained spotter reported that hay bales had been rolled over 100 ft across a field with thunderstorm winds. The nearby ASOS at Watertown Regional Airport recorded a peak wind gust of 68 mph.
A trained spotter reported numerous tree branches up to 6 inches in diameter had come down. Some had blown nearly 100 feet across into a field.
The Codington County Emergency Manager reported multiple trees had been snapped due to strong thunderstorm winds. An empty grain bin had also been blown open at this location.

The Codington County Emergency manager reports water has filled the ditches and is up to the bottoms of several bridges on the main highways with water over some secondary roads northeast of Watertown. Photos were also submitted via Facebook of flooded residences in northeast Watertown.

Roberts County Emergency Management reports that barricades were required at several  locations where water has come up over highways and secondary roads, from portions of highway 15 near Wilmot all the way up to 123rd St 3 miles north of Agency Village.
Hail caused some minor crop damage. Thunderstorm winds also stripped a few 3 to 4 inch diameter tree branches down.
Minor tree damage in Huron with one tree that fell on a garage.
A trained spotter estimated winds topped 60 mph resulting in bent trees and several fallen  branches.
Thunderstorm winds downed a large tree branch along Faculty Drive.
Nickel size hail was accompanied by small branches down in Lake Preston City Park.
Thunderstorm winds downed a tree along U.S. Highway 14 near the South Dakota/Minnesota border.
A large tree limb was also blown down by thunderstorm winds.

Mud Creek at Rauville would go into flood during the early morning hours of August 6th, cresting in the late morning 1.34 feet above flood stage, before dropping below flood on August 7th in the afternoon.

events.county: Coastal Waters From Southwest Pass Of The Mississippi River To Port Fourchon Louisiana Out 20 Nm
events.narrative: Broadcast media relayed a picture from a waterspout south the Grand Isle coast.
Flash flooding was reported near the intersection of West Chatham and Fallsworth Drive. The road was impassable.

The South Branch Tributary of Mud Creek near Rauville went into flood during the morning hours of August 6th. A peak crest of 4.91 feet was recorded at 1045 am CST on August 6th, with the creek falling below flood stage on the afternoon of August 7th.
VDOT reported water over the roadway on Goodes Ferry Road.
VDOT reported water over the roadway on Virginia Route 473 (Buckly Road).

The portion of the Big Sioux River at Watertown Sioux Conifer Road went into flood at 845 am CST August 7th, cresting at 9.15 feet, or 0.15 feet above flood stage. The river fell below flood at 9 pm CST August 7th with the flooding primarily limited to low spots.
A 24 hour rain total of 4.8 inches.
Event total rainfall of 3.07 inches from personal weather station.
VDOT reported water over the roadway on Reavis Gin Road.
Crabtree Creek at Wake Forest Road exceeded minor flood stage.
Hail ranged in size up to quarter size.
Willow Creek near Watertown would go into flood on the morning of August 6th, cresting at 10.88 feet, or 0.88 above flood stage by the afternoon, and drop below flood stage by that evening.

The Big Sioux River near Watertown would go into flood around mid-day on August 6th, reaching 10.65 feet, or 0.65 feet above flood stage on the evening of the 6th. This portion of the river would remain in flood through the morning of the 7th. Flooding would mainly impact agricultural lands.
The road was closed due to water rushing across Olive Chapel Road in Apex.

The Big Sioux River near Castlewood entered flood stage around mid-day on August 6th. The river would crest at 1030 pm on August 7th at 10.63 feet, or 1.63 feet above flood stage. The river stayed in flood through the morning of August 10th. Flooding was mainly confined to low-lying agricultural lands north of Castlewood, though a portion of 184th street flooded.
Several roads were flooded in the Spring Hope area. Several cars were also stalled in flood waters.
The road was washed out near the intersection of Goldston Carbonton Road and Alton Kind Road.
Two people died after their vehicle was swept off North Carolina Highway 581 and into a ravine or ditch that was overflowing with fast moving flood waters.
VDOT reported standing water on Virginia Route 672 (Western Mill Road) near Triplet Road.
High water was reported on a couple of streets near the Ohio River.
WeatherFlow site XCBN Clam Bayou Nature Park reported a 44 mph wind gust.
Osage drive was flooded and impassable.
Several private weather stations in Orange Park measured near 3 inches of rain in the past hour.
